title: Blog 1
content:
Designing a Resilient Multi-Region Event Processing System on AWS with Amazon EventBridge and Amazon Route 53 When an application is deployed in only one AWS Region, a major failure in that Region can disrupt the entire service. This is particularly concerning for event-driven systems, such as order processing, transaction updates, and user activity tracking, where high availability and data durability are essential.
To reduce these risks, organizations can implement a Multi-Region architecture in which one Region serves as the primary environment while another is prepared as a standby environment. By combining Amazon Route 53, Amazon API Gateway, Amazon EventBridge, Amazon SQS, AWS Lambda, and Amazon DynamoDB Global Tables, the system can redirect new requests to the standby Region when the primary Region experiences a failure.
KEY POINTS TO UNDERSTAND Multi-Region Architecture: Deploying an application across multiple AWS Regions to improve availability and support disaster recovery. Active-Passive: Using the Primary Region to handle normal traffic while the Secondary Region serves as a standby environment. Amazon Route 53: Using Health Checks and Failover Routing Policy to monitor endpoints and route DNS queries to the appropriate Region. Event-Driven Processing: API Gateway receives requests, EventBridge routes events, SQS stores messages, and Lambda processes them. DynamoDB Global Tables: Maintaining data replicas across multiple AWS Regions through cross-Region replication. Automatic Failover: When the Primary Region fails to meet Health Check conditions, Route 53 can direct new DNS queries to the Secondary Region. Data Consistency: Considering replication latency, write conflicts, and duplicate message processing. 1. ARCHITECTURE OVERVIEW Multi-Region Architecture is an application deployment model that uses multiple AWS Regions to reduce dependence on a single infrastructure location. This solution adopts an Active-Passive model consisting of:
Primary Region: The main Region that receives and processes requests under normal operating conditions. Secondary Region: The standby Region, where the necessary components are pre-deployed to handle requests when the Primary Region experiences a failure. In addition, the system uses Event-Driven Architecture (EDA), which allows components to communicate through events rather than relying on direct interactions with one another. This approach separates request reception, event routing, and data processing while allowing individual components to scale independently.
2. AWS SERVICES AND THEIR ROLES AWS Service Role Amazon Route 53 Manages DNS, monitors endpoint health, and performs Failover Routing. Amazon API Gateway Receives HTTP/HTTPS requests and forwards events to EventBridge. Amazon EventBridge Receives events through an Event Bus and routes them according to Event Rules. Amazon SQS Stores messages in queues until they are ready for processing. AWS Lambda Retrieves messages from SQS, processes business logic, and writes data to DynamoDB. Amazon DynamoDB Global Tables Replicates data across AWS Regions. Amazon Route 53 – DNS Failover
Route 53 uses Health Checks to monitor the availability of the endpoint in the Primary Region. When the endpoint no longer meets the health check conditions, the Failover Routing Policy allows Route 53 to return the Secondary Region’s endpoint for new DNS queries.
Amazon API Gateway and Amazon EventBridge
API Gateway serves as the entry point for application requests. Through AWS Service Integration and the PutEvents API, API Gateway forwards event data to EventBridge. EventBridge receives the events, evaluates the configured Event Rules, and routes matching events to their designated targets.
Amazon SQS and AWS Lambda
SQS acts as an intermediate message queue, separating event reception from event processing. Lambda uses Event Source Mapping to retrieve messages from SQS in batches and execute the corresponding business logic.
Amazon DynamoDB Global Tables
Global Tables maintain replicas of the same DynamoDB table across multiple Regions. When data is written to one replica, the changes are replicated to the other replicas according to the configured consistency mode.
3. ARCHITECTURE AND OPERATIONAL FLOW 3.1. Overall Architecture The solution deploys two independent event-processing pipelines across two AWS Regions. Each Region contains API Gateway, EventBridge, SQS, and Lambda components. Route 53 manages DNS routing, while DynamoDB Global Tables handle data replication between the two Regions.
Architecture Diagram:
Figure 1. Multi-Region failover architecture using Amazon Route 53 and AWS serverless services.
The main processing flow in each Region is:
Amazon API Gateway → Amazon EventBridge → Amazon SQS → AWS Lambda → Amazon DynamoDB
3.2. Normal Operating Conditions When the Primary Region is operating normally, Route 53 resolves the domain name and prioritizes the endpoint of the primary environment.
Processing flow:
A user sends a request to the application domain name, and Route 53 resolves it to the Primary Region. API Gateway receives the request and sends the event to EventBridge through the PutEvents API. EventBridge evaluates the Event Rules and routes matching events to SQS. Lambda retrieves messages from SQS in batches through Event Source Mapping. Lambda processes the events and writes the results to the DynamoDB replica in the Primary Region. DynamoDB Global Tables replicate the data changes to the replica in the Secondary Region. 3.3. When the Primary Region Experiences a Failure When the Primary Region no longer meets the Health Check conditions, Route 53 updates its health status and applies the Failover Routing Policy.
Processing flow:
Route 53 Health Check detects that the Primary Region endpoint is unhealthy. Route 53 switches to the Secondary Record for new DNS queries. Users are routed to the API Gateway endpoint in the Secondary Region. EventBridge receives and routes events to the SQS queue in the standby Region. Lambda in the Secondary Region processes the messages and writes data to its local DynamoDB replica. Because the necessary components have already been deployed, the Secondary Region can continue receiving and processing new requests without rebuilding the entire system.
3.4. When the Primary Region Recovers When the Primary Region endpoint becomes healthy again and passes the Health Check, Route 53 can resume prioritizing the Primary Record for new DNS queries.
The process of directing traffic back to the primary environment is called Failback. However, users may continue using previously resolved DNS records for some time because of DNS caching and TTL settings. Therefore, the transition does not necessarily happen simultaneously across all devices.
4. DATA REPLICATION WITH DYNAMODB GLOBAL TABLES DynamoDB Global Tables maintain data across multiple Regions, allowing applications to access local replicas when another Region experiences a failure.
Global Tables currently support two main consistency modes:
Multi-Region Eventual Consistency (MREC): The default mode when no alternative consistency mode is specified. Data is replicated asynchronously across Regions, so there may be a delay before all replicas receive the latest changes. Multi-Region Strong Consistency (MRSC): Provides strong consistency across Regions, subject to AWS deployment requirements and limitations. In the original AWS architecture example, the CloudFormation configuration creates replicas without explicitly specifying another consistency mode. Therefore, the default MREC mode is applied.
Several important considerations include:
Replication Lag: The delay between the time data is written and the time it becomes available in another Region’s replica. Write Conflict: Conflicts that may occur when the same record is updated simultaneously in multiple Regions. Data Consistency: Data across Regions may temporarily differ while replication is still in progress. Recovery Point Objective (RPO): The amount of data loss an application can tolerate in the event of a failure. Therefore, it should not be assumed that every piece of data written to the Primary Region is immediately replicated to the Secondary Region.
5. DEPLOYMENT AND FAILOVER TESTING To deploy the solution according to the AWS guide, the following prerequisites are required:
An AWS account with permissions to manage the related services. AWS CLI and AWS SAM CLI installed and configured. A registered domain name and a Route 53 Hosted Zone. Appropriate ACM certificates in both Regions if Regional Custom Domains are used. Two selected AWS Regions designated as Primary and Secondary. General Deployment Process:
Deploy Primary Stack: Create API Gateway, EventBridge, SQS, Lambda, Route 53 Health Check, Primary DNS Record, and the DynamoDB Global Table with the required replicas. Deploy Secondary Stack: Create an independent processing pipeline in the standby Region and reference the existing DynamoDB Global Table. Verify Normal Operation: Send an event to the Custom Domain and confirm that the request is received by the Primary Region. Simulate a Failure: Make the Primary API Gateway endpoint fail its Health Check in the testing environment. Verify Failover: Send another request and check whether the system has switched to the Secondary Region. Verify Data: Review Lambda CloudWatch Logs and confirm that the record has been written to the DynamoDB replica in the Secondary Region. Restore the Primary Region: Restore the API Gateway Stage and Base Path Mapping, then verify that Route 53 can prioritize the Primary Region again. Example of Sending a Test Event:
curl -X POST https://api.example.com \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "Detail": { "IsHelloWorldExample": "true" }, "DetailType": "POSTED", "Source": "demo.event" }' -v According to the AWS example, the HTTP response includes an X-Region header that identifies the Region handling the request. Under normal conditions, the result indicates the Primary Region. After a successful Failover, the result indicates the Secondary Region.
Note: With the example Health Check configuration using a 30-second interval and a Failure Threshold of 3, the failure detection threshold is approximately 90 seconds. However, the actual failover time also depends on DNS TTL and DNS Resolver caching.
6. BENEFITS AND IMPORTANT CONSIDERATIONS Benefits:
Improved Availability: Reduces dependence on a single AWS Region. Disaster Recovery Support: Provides a standby environment when the primary Region experiences a failure. Reduced Component Coupling: EventBridge and SQS help separate event reception from event processing. Multi-Region Data Availability: DynamoDB Global Tables replicate data across Regions. Simplified Infrastructure Management: AWS SAM and CloudFormation support infrastructure deployment through Infrastructure as Code. Important Considerations:
DNS Failover Is Not Instantaneous: DNS Resolvers may continue using previously cached DNS records until their TTL expires. Appropriate Health Checks: The monitored endpoint should accurately reflect the application’s actual service availability. Duplicate Message Processing: Lambda and SQS may process a message more than once. Applications should implement Idempotent processing logic and consider using a Dead-Letter Queue. Data Replication Monitoring: ReplicationLatency should be monitored for Global Tables using MREC. IAM Access Control: Permissions should follow the Least Privilege principle. Cost Monitoring: Costs should account for API Gateway, Route 53 Health Checks, DynamoDB Global Tables, Lambda, SQS, CloudWatch Logs, and cross-Region data transfer. After completing the testing process, it is recommended to delete the Secondary Stack first, followed by the Primary Stack, according to the AWS deployment guide. In particular, important data should be backed up because deleting the Primary Stack may also delete the Global Table and its stored data.
7. CONCLUSION The Multi-Region Event-Driven Failover architecture, combining Amazon EventBridge and Amazon Route 53, is a solution that helps improve availability and disaster recovery capabilities for event-driven applications on AWS.
In this architecture, Route 53 monitors endpoint health and manages DNS routing between the Primary and Secondary Regions. API Gateway receives requests, EventBridge routes events, SQS stores messages, Lambda processes business logic, and DynamoDB Global Tables maintain data replicas across the deployed Regions.
This architecture demonstrates that building a standby system involves more than simply deploying an additional Region. The processing components, data replication mechanisms, and failover procedures must also be properly prepared and coordinated.
However, before applying this architecture in a production environment, organizations should evaluate RTO, RPO, DNS TTL, data replication latency, and duplicate message handling. These factors determine whether the architecture is suitable for the operational requirements of a particular application.

Week 1 Objectives: Get acquainted with members of First Cloud AI Journey and understand the internship program’s rules, regulations, requirements, and weekly learning roadmap. Understand the AWS Free Tier 2025 program, including its major changes, account plans, promotional credits, eligibility conditions, and account protection policies. Learn the AWS account registration process, explore the AWS Management Console, and understand how to manage account information and promotional credits. Understand AWS Budgets and its four budget types, including budget configurations, monitoring periods, usage limits, and cost alert notifications. Gain practical experience in creating and configuring AWS Budgets to monitor cloud service costs and resource usage, helping prevent unexpected AWS charges. Tasks to be carried out this week: Day Task Start Date Completion Date Reference Material 2 - Get acquainted with members of First Cloud AI Journey.
- Read and understand the internship program’s rules, regulations, requirements, and working procedures.
- Review the internship learning roadmap and understand the main topics, objectives, and activities planned for each week. 05/10/2026 05/10/2026 3 - Study AWS Free Tier 2025 and understand the major changes introduced from July 15, 2025, compared to the previous Free Tier program.
- Learn about the two AWS account plans: Free Account Plan and Paid Account Plan.
- Understand the $100 initial credit granted upon registration and the additional $100 credit obtainable by completing five specified learning tasks.
- Study the benefits and limitations of the Free Account Plan, including the six-month protection period, automatic account closure conditions, and access to more than 30 Always Free services.
- Understand the Paid Account Plan, including full access to AWS services, promotional credit eligibility, short-term service trials, and charges that may apply when usage exceeds available credits.

- Learn about account setup, including email verification, account information, password configuration, account plan selection, payment method verification, and phone number verification.
- Explore the AWS Management Console and become familiar with its interface, navigation, and main service categories.
- Learn how to access the Billing and Cost Management dashboard and locate promotional credit information.
- Understand how to check credit balances, credit expiration dates, eligibility conditions, and services covered by promotional credits.
- Recognize the importance of monitoring credit usage and reviewing AWS service consumption to avoid unexpected charges. 07/10/2026 07/10/2026 AWS Free Tier 2025 5 - Study AWS Budgets and understand its role in monitoring, managing, and controlling AWS cloud service costs.
- Learn about the four main types of AWS Budgets:
+ Cost Budget
+ Usage Budget
+ Reserved Instance (RI) Budget
+ Savings Plans Budget
- Understand the differences between Cost Budget, which monitors spending, and Usage Budget, which monitors resource consumption.
- Learn how Reserved Instance Budgets monitor Reserved Instance utilization and coverage, and how Savings Plans Budgets monitor Savings Plans utilization and commitments.
- Study budget configuration options, including daily, monthly, quarterly, and annual periods.
- Understand recurring and expiring budgets, as well as fixed and planned budget amounts.
- Learn how to configure alert thresholds for actual and forecasted costs and receive email notifications when budget limits are reached or exceeded.
- Explore AWS Budget templates, particularly the Monthly Cost Budget template, and learn how to customize budget configurations according to monitoring requirements. 08/10/2026 08/10/2026 AWS Budgets - Getting Started 6 - Practice: Create and configure an AWS Budget through AWS Billing and Cost Management.
+ Access the AWS Management Console and open the Billing and Cost Management service.
+ Navigate to Budgets and select Create a budget.
+ Explore the available budget creation methods and templates.
+ Create a Monthly Cost Budget using the predefined template.
+ Specify the budget name, monthly spending limit, monitoring period, and alert thresholds.
+ Configure email notifications to receive alerts when the budget thresholds are reached or exceeded.
+ Explore customized Cost Budget settings, including budget periods, recurring or expiring budgets, and fixed or planned budget amounts.
+ Explore Usage Budget configuration and learn how to monitor EC2 running hours using the EC2: ELB - Running Hours usage type group, where available.
+ Review budget configurations, budget status, budget health, and budget history.
- Learn how to delete temporary test budgets after completing the exercises to avoid unnecessary notifications.
- Understand that deleting a budget removes its monitoring and alert configuration but does not automatically delete or stop running AWS resources. 09/10/2026 09/10/2026 AWS Budgets - Getting Started Week 1 Achievements: Became familiar with the members of First Cloud AI Journey, the internship program’s rules, regulations, requirements, and weekly learning roadmap.
Gained a comprehensive understanding of the AWS Free Tier 2025 program and its major improvements compared to the previous Free Tier model, particularly for accounts created from July 15, 2025, including:
$100 initial credit upon account registration. Additional $100 credit through five specified learning tasks, with $20 associated with each task. Two available account plans: Free Account Plan and Paid Account Plan. Six-month protection period under the Free Account Plan, subject to the program’s applicable conditions. Access to more than 30 Always Free services within their applicable free usage limits. Differences in account expiration and automatic closure between the two plans. Understood the differences between the Free Account Plan and Paid Account Plan, particularly in terms of:
AWS service availability and access restrictions. Promotional credit usage and eligibility. Billing responsibilities when usage exceeds available credits. Account protection and automatic closure conditions. Availability of additional promotional credits and short-term service trials. Gained knowledge of the AWS account registration process, including:
Providing account information and configuring account credentials. Verifying the registration email. Selecting an appropriate account plan. Providing and verifying payment information. Verifying the registered phone number. Selecting the applicable support plan. Became familiar with the AWS Management Console and learned how to navigate the interface, search for AWS services, and access the Billing and Cost Management dashboard.
Understood how to check promotional credits through the AWS Billing Console, including:
Reviewing available credit balances. Checking credit expiration dates. Understanding credit eligibility conditions. Identifying services covered by promotional credits. Monitoring credit consumption to avoid unexpected charges. Gained a comprehensive understanding of AWS Budgets and its four main budget types:
Cost Budget: Monitors actual and forecasted AWS spending against a specified budget amount and sends alerts when configured thresholds are reached or exceeded. Usage Budget: Monitors the consumption of selected AWS services against predefined usage limits, such as EC2 running hours. Reserved Instance (RI) Budget: Monitors Reserved Instance utilization and coverage to help track the usage of reserved capacity commitments. Savings Plans Budget: Monitors Savings Plans utilization and commitments to help track the usage of savings plan benefits. Understood the differences between Cost Budget and Usage Budget, particularly that Cost Budget focuses on monetary spending, whereas Usage Budget focuses on the actual consumption of AWS resources.
Gained knowledge of AWS Budget configuration options, including:
Selecting an appropriate budget type. Configuring daily, monthly, quarterly, and annual monitoring periods. Setting fixed or planned budget amounts. Configuring recurring or expiring budgets. Defining budget scopes and the AWS services to be monitored. Setting actual and forecasted cost alert thresholds. Configuring email notifications when budget thresholds are reached or exceeded. Became familiar with AWS Budget templates and learned how to use the predefined Monthly Cost Budget template to simplify budget creation and configuration.
Gained practical experience in creating and configuring an AWS Cost Budget through the AWS Billing and Cost Management console, including:
Accessing the Budgets management interface. Selecting an appropriate budget creation method. Configuring a monthly spending limit. Setting alert thresholds and email notifications. Reviewing the created budget and its configuration. Learned how to configure and monitor Usage Budgets, particularly how to select the EC2: ELB - Running Hours usage type group to monitor EC2 instance running hours.
Understood how to review budget status, budget health, and budget history to monitor spending and resource consumption over time.
Learned the importance of AWS cost management and resource cleanup, including deleting temporary test budgets after completing practical exercises to avoid unnecessary notifications.
Recognized that AWS Budget alerts are monitoring and notification mechanisms. They do not automatically stop running AWS resources or prevent additional service charges when a budget threshold is exceeded.

Week 2 Objectives: Learn about AWS Support and its role in providing technical, account, and billing assistance during the management and operation of AWS services. Understand the four AWS Support plans: Basic, Business Support+, Enterprise Support, and Unified Operations, including their features, support channels, service levels, and response times. Understand the three main types of AWS Support requests: Account and Billing Support, Service Limit Increase, and Technical Support. Learn how to access AWS Support, manage support plans, create Support Cases, select appropriate severity levels, and monitor submitted requests through AWS Support Center. Understand AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) and its role in managing user identities, access permissions, and security within an AWS account. Learn about the main IAM components, including IAM User, IAM Group, IAM Policy, and IAM Role, and understand how to organize users and manage permissions according to the Principle of Least Privilege. Gain practical knowledge and experience in creating and managing IAM Groups, IAM Users, and IAM Roles, configuring access policies, and performing role switching (Switch Role) through the AWS Management Console. Develop practical skills in handling AWS Support requests and managing IAM access permissions while following security best practices and avoiding unnecessary AWS service costs. Tasks to be carried out this week: Day Task Start Date Completion Date Reference Material 2 - Study the fundamentals of AWS Support and understand its role in providing account, billing, and technical assistance to AWS customers.
- Learn about the four AWS Support plans and their main features:
+ Basic: Provides basic account and billing assistance, AWS Support Forums, AWS Health Dashboard, and access to AWS documentation and guidance resources.
+ Business Support+: Provides 24/7 access to Cloud Support Engineers, unlimited support cases, AWS Trusted Advisor checks, AWS Support API, and third-party software support.
+ Enterprise Support: Includes Business Support+ features, Technical Account Manager (TAM), Concierge Support Team, Infrastructure Event Management, Well-Architected Reviews, and operational guidance.
+ Unified Operations: Includes Enterprise Support features and AWS Managed Services, proactive monitoring, incident management, change management, patch management, backup, and disaster recovery support.
- Compare the support plans in terms of service availability, support channels, additional features, and response times.
- Learn about the three main types of AWS Support requests:
+ Account and Billing Support: Assistance with account and billing-related issues.
+ Service Limit Increase: Requests to increase AWS service quotas.
+ Technical Support: Assistance with technical issues.
- Understand which types of support requests are available under the Basic plan and which require an upgraded support plan.
- Become familiar with AWS Support Center and learn how to access support services through the AWS Management Console.
- Learn how to change support plans through the Manage Support Plan section.
- Understand the additional monthly costs that may arise when upgrading from the Basic plan to paid support plans. 12/10/2026 12/10/2026 AWS Support - Request Support 3 - Study AWS Support request management and understand how AWS Support Center is used to create, manage, and track Support Cases.
- Learn how to identify the appropriate support request type for different issues:
+ Account and Billing Support: Handles issues related to invoices, payments, account verification, account information changes, and tax-related questions.
+ Service Limit Increase: Allows customers to request increases to default AWS service quotas according to their resource requirements.
+ Technical Support: Provides technical assistance for AWS services and third-party applications running on AWS, depending on the subscribed support plan.
- Learn about the severity levels used when submitting technical support requests:
+ General Guidance: General development questions or feature requests.
+ System Impaired: Non-critical application functionality is affected or not operating normally.
+ Production System Impaired: Important functionality of a production system is impaired or degraded.
+ Production System Down: Important production system functionality is unavailable.
+ Business-Critical System Down: Critical system functionality is unavailable, potentially causing serious disruption to business operations.
- Learn about the initial response times associated with different severity levels and applicable support plans.
- Study how to provide a clear subject, detailed issue description, relevant attachments, and required account information when creating a Support Case.
- Understand the importance of selecting an appropriate severity level and avoiding the disclosure of sensitive information such as passwords and AWS Access Keys.

IoT Weather Platform for Lab Research A Unified AWS Serverless Solution for Real-Time Weather Monitoring 1. Executive Summary 2. Problem Statement What’s the Problem? The Solution Benefits and Return on Investment 3. Solution Architecture The platform employs a serverless AWS architecture to manage data from 5 Raspberry Pi-based stations, scalable to 15. Data is ingested via AWS IoT Core, stored in an S3 data lake, and processed by AWS Glue Crawlers and ETL jobs to transform and load it into another S3 bucket for analysis. Lambda and API Gateway handle additional processing, while Amplify with Next.js hosts the dashboard, secured by Cognito. The architecture is detailed below:
AWS Services Used AWS IoT Core: Ingests MQTT data from 5 stations, scalable to 15. AWS Lambda: Processes data and triggers Glue jobs (two functions). Amazon API Gateway: Facilitates web app communication. Amazon S3: Stores raw data in a data lake and processed outputs (two buckets). AWS Glue: Crawlers catalog data, and ETL jobs transform and load it. AWS Amplify: Hosts the Next.js web interface. Amazon Cognito: Secures access for lab users. Component Design Edge Devices: Raspberry Pi collects and filters sensor data, sending it to IoT Core. Data Ingestion: AWS IoT Core receives MQTT messages from the edge devices. Data Storage: Raw data is stored in an S3 data lake; processed data is stored in another S3 bucket. Data Processing: AWS Glue Crawlers catalog the data, and ETL jobs transform it for analysis. Web Interface: AWS Amplify hosts a Next.js app for real-time dashboards and analytics. User Management: Amazon Cognito manages user access, allowing up to 5 active accounts. 4. Technical Implementation Implementation Phases This project has two parts—setting up weather edge stations and building the weather platform—each following 4 phases:
Build Theory and Draw Architecture: Research Raspberry Pi setup with ESP32 sensors and design the AWS serverless architecture (1 month pre-internship) Calculate Price and Check Practicality: Use AWS Pricing Calculator to estimate costs and adjust if needed (Month 1). Fix Architecture for Cost or Solution Fit: Tweak the design (e.g., optimize Lambda with Next.js) to stay cost-effective and usable (Month 2). Develop, Test, and Deploy: Code the Raspberry Pi setup, AWS services with CDK/SDK, and Next.js app, then test and release to production (Months 2-3). Technical Requirements
Weather Edge Station: Sensors (temperature, humidity, rainfall, wind speed), a microcontroller (ESP32), and a Raspberry Pi as the edge device. Raspberry Pi runs Raspbian, handles Docker for filtering, and sends 1 MB/day per station via MQTT over Wi-Fi. Weather Platform: Practical knowledge of AWS Amplify (hosting Next.js), Lambda (minimal use due to Next.js), AWS Glue (ETL), S3 (two buckets), IoT Core (gateway and rules), and Cognito (5 users). Use AWS CDK/SDK to code interactions (e.g., IoT Core rules to S3). Next.js reduces Lambda workload for the fullstack web app. 5. Timeline & Milestones Project Timeline
Pre-Internship (Month 0): 1 month for planning and old station review. Internship (Months 1-3): 3 months. Month 1: Study AWS and upgrade hardware. Month 2: Design and adjust architecture. Month 3: Implement, test, and launch. Post-Launch: Up to 1 year for research. 6. Budget Estimation You can find the budget estimation on the AWS Pricing Calculator.
Or you can download the Budget Estimation File.
Infrastructure Costs AWS Services: AWS Lambda: $0.00/month (1,000 requests, 512 MB storage). S3 Standard: $0.15/month (6 GB, 2,100 requests, 1 GB scanned). Data Transfer: $0.02/month (1 GB inbound, 1 GB outbound). AWS Amplify: $0.35/month (256 MB, 500 ms requests). Amazon API Gateway: $0.01/month (2,000 requests). AWS Glue ETL Jobs: $0.02/month (2 DPUs). AWS Glue Crawlers: $0.07/month (1 crawler). MQTT (IoT Core): $0.08/month (5 devices, 45,000 messages). Total: $0.7/month, $8.40/12 months
Hardware: $265 one-time (Raspberry Pi 5 and sensors). 7. Risk Assessment Risk Matrix Network Outages: Medium impact, medium probability. Sensor Failures: High impact, low probability. Cost Overruns: Medium impact, low probability. Mitigation Strategies Network: Local storage on Raspberry Pi with Docker. Sensors: Regular checks and spares. Cost: AWS budget alerts and optimization. Contingency Plans Revert to manual methods if AWS fails. Use CloudFormation for cost-related rollbacks. 8. Expected Outcomes Technical Improvements: Real-time data and analytics replace manual processes.
Scalable to 10-15 stations.
Long-term Value 1-year data foundation for AI research.
Reusable for future projects.

Week 3 Objectives: Understand the overview of Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) and its role in building and managing isolated virtual network environments on AWS. Understand basic networking concepts, including IP addresses, CIDR, Availability Zones, and how to divide a network into Subnets to organize AWS resources. Learn about the functions and operations of VPC networking components, including Subnets, Route Tables, Internet Gateway (IGW), and NAT Gateway. Understand network security mechanisms in VPC through Security Groups and Network Access Control Lists (Network ACLs), and distinguish their scopes and operating mechanisms. Gain practical knowledge and experience in creating VPCs, configuring Subnets, Internet Gateways, Route Tables, Security Groups, and VPC Flow Logs. Learn how to deploy Amazon EC2 Instances in Public and Private Subnets, establish SSH connections, configure NAT Gateways, and verify network connectivity. Become familiar with AWS network analysis and monitoring tools, including VPC Resource Map, VPC Reachability Analyzer, AWS Systems Manager Session Manager, and Amazon CloudWatch. Understand AWS Site-to-Site VPN and the principles of establishing secure network connectivity between an On-premises environment and Amazon VPC through encrypted VPN tunnels. Gain practical experience in configuring Virtual Private Gateway (VGW), Customer Gateway (CGW), VPN Connection, and Libreswan software to establish Site-to-Site VPN connectivity. Understand the procedures for monitoring VPN Tunnels, customizing connection parameters, troubleshooting connectivity issues, and cleaning up AWS resources to minimize unexpected costs. Tasks to be carried out this week: Day Task Start Date Completion Date Reference Material 2 - Study the overview of Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) and its role in creating isolated virtual network environments on AWS.
- Learn about VPC network architecture and its basic concepts:
+ VPC: An isolated virtual network in AWS that allows users to control network configurations and deploy resources.
+ CIDR: The range of IP addresses allocated to a VPC and its Subnets.
+ Availability Zone (AZ): An independent location within an AWS Region that supports high availability for deployed resources.
- Learn about different types of Subnets:
+ Public Subnet: A Subnet with a route to the Internet through an Internet Gateway.
+ Private Subnet: A Subnet without a direct route to an Internet Gateway.
+ VPN-only Subnet: A Subnet configured with routes to a Virtual Private Gateway for VPN connectivity.
- Study Route Tables and their routing components:
+ Destination: The destination IP address or network range of traffic.
+ Target: The gateway or network component to which traffic is forwarded.
- Learn about Internet Gateway (IGW), its function in connecting a VPC to the Internet, and how to configure IGW routes in a Route Table.
- Understand NAT Gateway and how it allows resources in Private Subnets to initiate outbound Internet connections without allowing the Internet to initiate direct connections to those resources.
- Distinguish between NAT Gateway and NAT Instance.
- Study Multi-AZ network architecture and the benefits of distributing resources across multiple Availability Zones to improve availability. 19/10/2026 19/10/2026 Amazon VPC and AWS Site-to-Site VPN Workshop 3 - Study network security mechanisms in Amazon VPC:
+ Security Group: A virtual firewall that controls inbound and outbound traffic at the Network Interface or associated resource level.
+ Network ACL (NACL): A network traffic control mechanism applied at the Subnet level.
- Understand the differences between Security Groups and Network ACLs in terms of scope and operating mechanisms:
+ Security Groups are Stateful, meaning response traffic for permitted connections is automatically allowed.
+ Network ACLs are Stateless, requiring rules for both inbound and outbound traffic.
- Learn about Inbound Rules and Outbound Rules, including how to specify protocols, Port Ranges, and Source/Destination addresses when configuring security rules.
- Become familiar with VPC Resource Map to visualize relationships between VPCs, Subnets, Route Tables, Internet Gateways, and related network components.

+ Access the VPC service and create a Custom VPC named ASG.

+ Create Public and Private Subnets in the selected Availability Zones.
+ Create an Internet Gateway and attach it to the ASG VPC.
+ Create a Route Table for the Public Subnet and configure the default route 0.0.0.0/0 to the Internet Gateway.
+ Associate the Subnets with their appropriate Route Tables.
+ Create a Security Group and configure Inbound Rules and Outbound Rules according to connectivity requirements.
+ Learn how to configure Network ACLs to control traffic at the Subnet level.

+ Test Internet connectivity for resources configured in Public Subnets.

+ Allocate an Elastic IP Address for the NAT Gateway.
+ Create a Public NAT Gateway in the appropriate Public Subnet.
+ Associate the NAT Gateway with the allocated Elastic IP Address.
+ Configure the Private Subnet Route Table with the default route 0.0.0.0/0 pointing to the NAT Gateway.

+ Virtual Private Gateway (VGW): The AWS-side VPN gateway attached to a VPC.
+ Customer Gateway (CGW): Represents the VPN device or software on the customer network side.
+ VPN Connection: The VPN connection established between a Virtual Private Gateway and a Customer Gateway.
+ VPN Tunnel: An encrypted communication tunnel used to securely transfer data between two network environments.

+ Create a Public Subnet and configure an Internet Gateway for the VPN environment.

- Learn about Amazon EC2, its functions, and the benefits of using virtual servers on AWS Cloud.
- Learn about different EC2 Instance Types and the factors affecting performance, such as CPU, RAM, Storage, and Network Performance.
- Learn about Amazon Machine Images (AMIs), Amazon EBS, Instance Store, Key Pairs, and Security Groups.
- Practice creating separate VPCs for Linux and Windows environments. For the Linux VPC, select the “VPC and more” configuration, set up 2 Availability Zones, 2 Public Subnets, and 2 Private Subnets, and do not create VPC Endpoints during the workshop.
- Enable automatic Public IPv4 address assignment for Public Subnets to support connections to EC2 Instances.
- Create separate Security Groups for Linux and Windows, and configure the corresponding Inbound Rules based on access requirements, including SSH (22), HTTP (80), HTTPS (443), RDP (3389), MySQL (3306), Custom TCP (5000), and ICMP.
- Learn the Least Privilege security principle by allowing only necessary ports and restricting access sources appropriately. 26/10/2026 26/10/2026 Introduction to Amazon EC2 3 Launch EC2 Instances and Practice Connecting to Windows/Linux Servers

- Learn about Amazon Machine Images (AMIs) and practice creating a Custom AMI from a configured Windows Server 2025 Instance.

- Learn about the architecture and functionality of the AWS User Management application, which is built with Node.js, Express.js, Handlebars, and MySQL, and supports CRUD (Create, Read, Update, Delete) operations on user data.

- Use Git to clone the application source code from the repository https://github.com/First-Cloud-Journey/000004-EC2.git.
- Initialize and configure the Node.js project using NPM, and install the required libraries, including Express, dotenv, express-handlebars, body-parser, and mysql.
- Create and configure the .env file to specify the MySQL database connection settings. Start the application using the npm start command and access it through the EC2 Public DNS combined with port 5000.
- Continue practicing application deployment on Windows Server 2025 by installing XAMPP and Node.js, initializing the project, installing dependencies, and configuring the database connection.
- Start the application on Windows Server and access its interface through http://localhost:5000 to verify that it works correctly.
- Test the CRUD functions by adding a new user and checking the user list after the data has been updated.
- Learn how to check and resolve Node.js library security warnings using npm update, npm audit fix, and updating Nodemon when necessary. 29/10/2026 29/10/2026 Introduction to Amazon EC2 6 Learn About and Practice Granting Applications Access to AWS Using IAM Roles
- Learn about AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), including the roles of IAM Users, Access Keys, Secret Access Keys, IAM Policies, and IAM Roles in managing access to AWS services.
- Practice creating an EC2 Instance using Amazon Linux with the t2.micro configuration, following the Workshop instructions, and connecting to the server using PuTTY.
- Create an Amazon S3 Bucket for data storage and verify that the Bucket has been created successfully.

- Learn how to use the Access Key ID and Secret Access Key in a Python application with the Boto3 library to upload files to an S3 Bucket.
- Understand the security risks of storing Access Keys and Secret Access Keys directly in application source code, especially the risk of exposing credentials.
- Practice creating an IAM Role named EC2RoleS3Upload, selecting EC2 as the AWS Service, and attaching the AmazonS3FullAccess Policy to grant applications running on EC2 access to S3.
- Attach the EC2RoleS3Upload IAM Role to the EC2 Instance through Actions → Security → Modify IAM Role.
- Create a Python application using Boto3 with an S3 Client that does not require Access Keys or Secret Access Keys to be specified directly in the source code.
- Practice uploading files to S3 using the IAM Role and verify the results in the S3 Bucket to confirm that access permissions are working correctly.
- Compare the two access management methods using Access Keys and IAM Roles, and evaluate the security benefits of using IAM Roles when applications run on EC2.
- Clean up resources after the Workshop: delete the data and S3 Bucket, terminate the EC2 Instance, delete the IAM User, deactivate/delete the Access Key, and delete the IAM Role that was created.

Secure Hybrid Access to S3 using VPC Endpoints Overview AWS PrivateLink provides private connectivity to AWS services from VPCs and your on-premises networks, without exposing your traffic to the Public Internet.
In this lab, you will learn how to create, configure, and test VPC endpoints that enable your workloads to reach AWS services without traversing the Public Internet.
You will create two types of endpoints to access Amazon S3: a Gateway VPC endpoint, and an Interface VPC endpoint. These two types of VPC endpoints offer different benefits depending on if you are accessing Amazon S3 from the cloud or your on-premises location
Gateway - Create a gateway endpoint to send traffic to Amazon S3 or DynamoDB using private IP addresses.You route traffic from your VPC to the gateway endpoint using route tables. Interface - Create an interface endpoint to send traffic to endpoint services that use a Network Load Balancer to distribute traffic. Traffic destined for the endpoint service is resolved using DNS.
